items.question_text: A GP has been seeing a 32-year-old woman for depression for six months. She is improving. He asks whether he may now begin a sexual relationship with her, because the therapeutic relationship is almost over. A sexual relationship with a current or recent patient is professional misconduct. The end of the formal treating period does not make it acceptable. What is the most appropriate view?  Six months of care for depression is a current treating relationship. Almost over is not over, and recent is still prohibited. Decline the relationship.  The standard is the same whether or not anyone complains. Apply it to the facts in front of you.  A private arrangement or a past illness does not create an exception here.  Decide on the duty, not on convenience.  Nothing in the history lowers the standard. The same rule applies if the person is a friend, a colleague, or a relative.  Act on the duty now. Waiting for a complaint is not the safeguard.  That is the professional response. Do not delay it. Today. Clearly.
options: A sexual relationship with a current or recent patient is misconduct, and transfer does not immediately cure it
A relationship is acceptable once care is transferred and she consents
It is acceptable because he is not her surgeon
It is acceptable if it is not recorded in the notes
Only a relationship with a patient under 18 is misconduct
items.subtopic: A sexual or improper relationship with a patient is professional misconduct, even if the patient agrees.
items.lo_title: A sexual relationship with a current or recent patient is misconduct

blueprint.note: Coverage reporting and tie-break only. Not a quota.

items.explanation:
The power imbalance of a treating relationship means a sexual relationship with a patient is misconduct. Ending the formal relationship yesterday does not remove that imbalance, especially after long psychological care. Consent does not cure it.

B. A relationship is acceptable once care is transferred and she consents
Transfer and consent do not repair the boundary.

A. A sexual relationship with a current or recent patient is misconduct, and transfer does not immediately cure it
This is the view.

C. It is acceptable because he is not her surgeon
The rule is not limited to surgeons.

D. It is acceptable if it is not recorded in the notes
Concealment makes it worse.

E. Only a relationship with a patient under 18 is misconduct
Adult patients are protected too.
items.diagnosis_explanation: Do not start the relationship. Consent and a transfer do not make it acceptable.
key_takeaways: A sexual relationship with a patient is misconduct.
Consent does not cure the power imbalance.

What is the most appropriate action?  Alcohol on the breath before an anaesthetic is a current risk. Two drinks last night is not a clearance. Stand him down from the list. Notification may follow.  The standard is the same whether or not anyone complains. Apply it to the facts in front of you.  A private arrangement or a past illness does not create an exception here.  Decide on the duty, not on convenience.  Nothing in the history lowers the standard. The same rule applies if the person is a friend, a colleague, or a relative.  Act on the duty now. Waiting for a complaint is not the safeguard.  That is the professional response. Do not delay it. Today. Clearly.
options: Cover the rest of his shift and say nothing
Stop him seeing patients now, correct the risk, and make a mandatory notification
Wait until the end of the term before deciding
Tell only the other registrars in a group chat
Accept his plan to sleep if he promises not to prescribe again tonight
items.subtopic: Practising while intoxicated is a mandatory notification. Friendship is not a reason to stay silent.
items.lo_title: Impairment that risks patients is acted on at once

blueprint.note: Coverage reporting and tie-break only. Not a quota.

items.explanation:
Intoxication while practising places patients at substantial risk. That is a ground for mandatory notification. The unsafe dose must be corrected and he must stop work now. A private promise is not a safeguard.

A. Cover the rest of his shift and say nothing
Silence leaves the next patient exposed.

B. Stop him seeing patients now, correct the risk, and make a mandatory notification
This is the action.

C. Wait until the end of the term before deciding
The risk is tonight.

D. Tell only the other registrars in a group chat
Gossip is not notification, and it spreads his health information.

E. Accept his plan to sleep if he promises not to prescribe again tonight
A promise from an intoxicated colleague is not protection.
items.diagnosis_explanation: Stop him now and notify. Friendship does not cover intoxication at work.
key_takeaways: Intoxicated practice is mandatorily notifiable.
Remove him from patient care immediately.

Suggest he operate only on private patients

Agree, provided he stops self-prescribing

items.diagnosis_explanation: He stops now. A retirement date is not a safety plan.

A private arrangement or a past illness does not create an exception here.  Decide on the duty, not on convenience.  Nothing in the history lowers the standard. The same rule applies if the person is a friend, a colleague, or a relative.  Act on the duty now. Waiting for a complaint is not the safeguard.  That is the professional response. Do not delay it. Today. Clearly.
options: Acceptable. No name means no breach
Acceptable if the account is set to friends only
Acceptable if posted more than an hour after the event
Acceptable because teaching justifies any de-identified image
A breach. The image and detail can identify him, and there is no consent

blueprint.note: Coverage reporting and tie-break only. Not a quota.

items.explanation:
Identification does not need a name. A distinctive tattoo plus a time and place can identify a patient. Posting it without consent is a breach, whatever the privacy setting.

A. Acceptable. No name means no breach
Name is not the only identifier.

E. A breach. The image and detail can identify him, and there is no consent
This is the judgment.

B. Acceptable if the account is set to friends only

C. Acceptable if posted more than an hour after the event

D. Acceptable because teaching justifies any de-identified image

items.diagnosis_explanation: Take it down. No name does not mean no identification.
key_takeaways: A case can be identified without a name.

He says he is in a hurry and the examination will only take a minute. A chaperone is offered, and a patient's request for one is respected. Stop. Offer to wait for the nurse or to rebook with a chaperone. What is the most appropriate action?  She asked for a nurse. Hurry is not a reason to proceed. Wait or rebook. Do not examine without the chaperone she requested.  The standard is the same whether or not anyone complains. Apply it to the facts in front of you.  A private arrangement or a past illness does not create an exception here.  Decide on the duty, not on convenience.  Nothing in the history lowers the standard. The same rule applies if the person is a friend, a colleague, or a relative.  Act on the duty now. Waiting for a complaint is not the safeguard.  That is the professional response. Do not delay it. Today. Clearly.
options: Stop. Offer to wait for the nurse or to rebook with a chaperone
Proceed. A short examination does not need a chaperone
Proceed if he leaves the door open
Ask her husband to wait outside and then proceed
Proceed and document that a chaperone was offered
items.subtopic: A chaperone is offered for an intimate examination. It is the patient's choice, not a formality.
items.lo_title: A chaperone request is respected

blueprint.note: Coverage reporting and tie-break only. Not a quota.

items.explanation:
She has asked for a chaperone. Proceeding without one, after that request, ignores her condition for the examination. An open door is not a chaperone. Documenting an offer she could not take up is not the same as providing one.

B. Proceed. A short examination does not need a chaperone
Length is irrelevant once she has asked.

A. Stop. Offer to wait for the nurse or to rebook with a chaperone
This is the course.

C. Proceed if he leaves the door open
An open door is not a chaperone.

D. Ask her husband to wait outside and then proceed
Sending the support person out is the opposite of her request.

E. Proceed and document that a chaperone was offered
The offer was accepted. Proceeding without one falsifies the protection.
items.diagnosis_explanation: Wait or rebook. Do not start because it will be quick.
key_takeaways: A requested chaperone is provided.
Documentation does not replace the person.

items.question_text: A surgeon's website says he has never had a complication from laparoscopic cholecystectomy in 2000 cases. A colleague knows of two bile-duct injuries. Advertising must not be misleading. An absolute claim of no complications, when complications have occurred, is misleading. What is the most appropriate view of the website?  Never had a complication is false if two bile-duct injuries occurred. Absolute claims in advertising are misleading. The website should not say it.  The standard is the same whether or not anyone complains. Apply it to the facts in front of you.  A private arrangement or a past illness does not create an exception here.  Decide on the duty, not on convenience.  Nothing in the history lowers the standard. The same rule applies if the person is a friend, a colleague, or a relative.  Act on the duty now. Waiting for a complaint is not the safeguard.  That is the professional response. Do not delay it. Today. Clearly.
options: Acceptable. Unnamed photos are always fair advertising
Misleading. An absolute claim of no complications is not acceptable
Acceptable if the photos are of real patients
Acceptable if a disclaimer is in small print
Acceptable because surgery advertising is unregulated
items.subtopic: Advertising must not create an unreasonable expectation. Before-and-after claims need care.
items.lo_title: Advertising must not be misleading

blueprint.note: Coverage reporting and tie-break only. Not a quota.

items.explanation:
Advertising must be honest and must not create an unreasonable expectation. A claim of no complications is misleading. Unnamed photos do not repair an absolute claim.

A. Acceptable. Unnamed photos are always fair advertising
Anonymity is not the problem.

B. Misleading. An absolute claim of no complications is not acceptable
This is the view.

C. Acceptable if the photos are of real patients
Real photos can still be misleading.

D. Acceptable if a disclaimer is in small print
Small print does not neutralise a false headline.

E. Acceptable because surgery advertising is unregulated
It is regulated.
items.diagnosis_explanation: The claim is misleading. No complications is not an acceptable promise.
key_takeaways: Advertising must not promise an outcome.
Small print does not repair a false claim.

Treating a close family member, especially for mental health or controlled drugs, is avoided. Decline to become her doctor. Arrange care with another practitioner. The standard is the same whether or not anyone complains. Apply it to the facts in front of you.  A private arrangement or a past illness does not create an exception here.  Decide on the duty, not on convenience.  Nothing in the history lowers the standard. The same rule applies if the person is a friend, a colleague, or a relative.  Act on the duty now. Waiting for a complaint is not the safeguard.  That is the professional response. Do not delay it. Today. Clearly.

Prescribe once, then transfer
Decline to become her doctor. Arrange care with an independent GP
Prescribe if you document that she is your partner
Order the bloods but leave the script to a pharmacist
items.subtopic: A close personal relationship with a colleague's patient still needs a boundary if you become their doctor.
items.lo_title: Avoid treating a close family member for mental health or controlled drugs

blueprint.note: Coverage reporting and tie-break only. Not a quota.

items.explanation:
Treating someone with whom you have a close relationship risks impaired judgment, especially for drugs of dependence. The right step is an independent doctor, not a one-off script.

A. Prescribe. Treating family is always acceptable for short courses
Short and dependence-forming is a poor combination.

C. Decline to become her doctor. Arrange care with an independent GP

B. Prescribe once, then transfer
The one-off is the problem.

D. Prescribe if you document that she is your partner

E. Order the bloods but leave the script to a pharmacist
Splitting the care does not create an independent doctor.
items.diagnosis_explanation: Do not prescribe. She needs her own GP.
key_takeaways: Do not treat someone close to you for drugs of dependence.

The standard is the same whether or not anyone complains. Apply it to the facts in front of you.  A private arrangement or a past illness does not create an exception here.  Decide on the duty, not on convenience.  Nothing in the history lowers the standard. The same rule applies if the person is a friend, a colleague, or a relative.  Act on the duty now. Waiting for a complaint is not the safeguard.  That is the professional response. Do not delay it. Today. Clearly.

Treat the reaction and say nothing if he recovers
Blame the nurse in the notes and move on
Treat the reaction, keep the original record, and disclose the error
Ask the family what they would prefer to be told

items.lo_title: Do not rewrite the original record to protect yourself

blueprint.note: Coverage reporting and tie-break only. Not a quota.

items.explanation:
The reaction is treated. The record stays accurate. The error is disclosed. Rewriting the chart is a false record. Waiting to see if he recovers does not change the duty.

A. Rewrite the chart, then mention it vaguely
Altering the record is misconduct.

D. Treat the reaction, keep the original record, and disclose the error
This is the action.

B. Treat the reaction and say nothing if he recovers
Recovery does not erase the error.

C. Blame the nurse in the notes and move on

items.diagnosis_explanation: Treat him, keep the chart, and tell them. Do not rewrite it.
key_takeaways: A harmful error is disclosed.

Ask him to add the consents now and backdate them
Do nothing unless a patient complains

items.lo_title: Research misconduct and missing consent are raised

items.explanation:
